beats.trigger: ## Security
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: The discipline is running the check, not waiting for certainty.
beats.got: I can't prove an agent is safe from its output, so I need a repeatable check.

beats.trigger: The Module 4 prework adds two reads: (1) personal skills as the package format that carries expertise into your agent, (2) agent risk layered on top of normal security work.
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: **Evaluate** residual risk: what's left after mitigation, and what future sessions need before they touch the system
beats.got: Six verbs, and I'm only partly sure what half of them mean yet.

beats.trigger: Name the thing you'd want to check before letting this near a real stakeholder.
beats.got: I don't know why the three deciding agents agreed, and that bothers me before I send it to the CFO.

beats.trigger: The goal is not to memorize the exact answer.
beats.got: A tool call is just text that crosses into action. Fine, but I don't need three prompts to see that.

beats.trigger: Would you bet your job on it being safe?
beats.got: I wouldn't bet my job on the pricing brief agent, and that feeling is meant to stay.

beats.trigger: The story works because classical software is deterministic (same input, same output).
beats.got: Old security works because software repeats itself, which agents don't.

beats.trigger: Your firewall doesn't see it because your firewall has never had to worry about persuasion.
beats.got: The attack is a normal-looking document that talks my agent into something, and the firewall can't catch that.

beats.trigger: The reusable check is the expert. The job is reading the reports with judgment.
beats.got: Assess, then pick one of five mitigations (scope, split, filter, gate, review). My job is judging the reports, not being the security expert.

beats.trigger: **Decide.** Accept the residual on record, or close the door.
beats.got: After a mitigation I write down what's left and either sign for it or close the door. Hoping isn't an option.

beats.trigger: More context makes a good answer likelier. Less access makes a bad answer smaller.
beats.got: More context makes good answers likelier, and less access makes bad answers smaller. I have to pick the trade and sign for it.

beats.trigger: It costs whoever sells you agents too, this training included: an agent that reaches less is a smaller thing to sell, and it is still the right call.
beats.got: The cheapest mitigation is not connecting the thing at all, and the training admits that works against its own sales.

beats.trigger: You can't buy certainty. You can run a loop.
beats.got: Nothing new. This is the same point as before, restated.

beats.trigger: A **skill** packages an expertise (rules, checklists, the moves an agent runs) into something the agent can load and use.
beats.got: A skill is a reusable how that the agent loads when the work matches.

beats.trigger: The raw run shows which rules can be checked from files and which ones need judgment, context, or a standing evidence check.
beats.got: Some policy rules can be checked from files and others need judgment, and the raw run showed me which.

beats.trigger: The reusable check is supposed to carry what matters in your system, not generic GDPR.
beats.got: I told it what actually matters in my pricing setup, and the check was built around that instead of a generic brochure.

beats.trigger: You'll get a lot of questions. The grill is wide on purpose: the agent probes both lenses and won't stop at one round.
beats.got: It builds a policy lens and an agent-risk lens, and I get asked a lot to get there.

beats.trigger: *"You choose. Optimise for what I can't steer."*
beats.got: Answer what I know, hand over the rest in one line, then check the four risk patterns are all there.

beats.trigger: The project skill loads in your next session in this training directory.
beats.got: I saved the check so it's there next session without me rebuilding it.

beats.trigger: The policy files are source material. The reusable check is the expert in the room.
beats.got: What I built today is a check, not a prompt, and it still works next week.

beats.trigger: The goal is not a clean bill of health.
beats.got: Load the check, run it against my module 3 system, mitigate once, and write down the residual.

beats.trigger: Do not run a toy verification on one file. The first loaded use is the real audit.
beats.got: Start a fresh session and see /security-audit in the list.

beats.trigger: Expect the reusable check to find things you did not think about, and to leave things "I can't tell" you thought were settled.
beats.got: The check finds things I missed and reopens things I thought were settled. The mismatch between its surprises and mine is data.

beats.trigger: Two different lenses; some risks will overlap, some will not.
beats.got: The ranked risk report shows what the agent could reach or be misled into, and I can interrogate each risk.

beats.trigger: Your gut is data here.
beats.got: I picked the risk that bugged me, the agent applied the fix, and what's left is in the report for me to accept.

beats.trigger: The narrow question the expert can actually answer is sitting in the report.
beats.got: Take legal a narrow question with the evidence attached, not the whole tangle.

beats.trigger: You must do the work.
beats.got: Nothing new. Production needs more than one mitigation.

beats.trigger: The unease that remains is what the loop is supposed to produce, not what it failed to remove.
beats.got: Nothing new. Same point as before, and the recipe and pattern counts were a lot to take in.

beats.trigger: the root instructions file now tells future sessions how to behave around the risk you found.
beats.got: The rules from the audit go into the instructions file, so the next session starts stricter.

beats.trigger: Give a teammate the skill, install it in their runtime, and they can call the same method without reconstructing your prompt history.
beats.got: A skill is a method I can hand to a teammate, which is what I need for my fourteen people.

beats.trigger: "I can't tell" is a real answer; closing it takes evidence.
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: "the missing organisational check was X."
beats.got: Homework: one sentence per case on what check was missing.

beats.trigger: Carry the risk discipline from this module into both cases: what check was missing around the agent's output?
beats.got: Two cases to read before next time.

take_homes: Safety isn't something I get a yes or no on. I run assess, mitigate, residual, decide, and write down what's left.
The reusable check (a skill with a policy lens and an agent-risk lens) is the thing I built, not a clever prompt. It runs again next week and a teammate can install it.
The best mitigation is the door I don't open. Giving the agent less access is cheaper than patching afterwards.

monday.move: Run the security-audit skill on the pilot-cohort brief agent and pick one risk to cut. Probably drop its access to the churn article source.
monday.who: Me, then show the residual to the pricing working group and legal
monday.when: Monday morning, before the next brief goes to the working group
monday.stop_condition: One mitigation applied and the residual written down and accepted by me
monday.blocker: My team has no shared place for the skill and context files. Everyone keeps their own copy, so fourteen people can't load the same check yet.

misconception.why: I came in thinking good use meant better prompts. Here the durable thing was a check with judgment built in, plus the instructions file. I still think prompts matter, but they're not where the leverage is.

one_line: Good one: I came out with a security check I can reuse on Monday, though the 'you never get certainty' point got said about four times.
